title.narrative: NIHR RIGHT Transforming the Treatment and Prevention of Leprosy and Buruli Ulcers

description.narrative:
A UK and low-and-middle-income-country (LMIC) partnership that aims to improve the treatment and prevention of Leprosy and Buruli ulcers in Nepal, India and Nigeria.
The project has three main aims: 1. To improve self-care in the community for patients who are at risk of recurring leprosy ulcers. 2. To better understand the needs of patients with Buruli Ulcers and the barriers to meeting those needs. 3. To evaluate new methods of clinical care for leprosy patients.

The first aim – supporting self-care / self-help for people in the community who are at risk of recurring leprosy ulcers – is based on an ‘implementation science’ approach where we will work across all three countries to: 1. Agree and share a set of guidelines to support the set and management of self-care in the community. 2. Build on these principles to support the design and evaluate local interventions in collaboration with communities, patients, clinicians and policy-makers.
The second aim is to conduct a health needs assessment for Buruli ulcer patients in Nigeria to identify barriers and facilitators to meeting those needs.
The third aim – developing new methods of clinical care – will ‘translate’ knowledge by selecting and conducting preliminary evaluations of treatments that have a good chance of being effective and cost-effective in improving care for leprosy patients. These may be: 1. Ideas that have been tried but not proven in leprosy. 2. Treatments that are effective in other ulcer conditions and hold promise for leprosy or BU. 3. New ideas emanating from the ‘science base’.
The project is designed to create, as an additional key output, an international ‘Community of Practice’ involving researchers, community and public contributors, clinicians, and policy makers. This community will be ideally prepared and situated to build on the accomplishments of this grant and continue to collaborate, share best practice, and innovate in care so that fewer people will be stigmatised by deformities and disabilities resulting from the two highly stigmatising diseases.

participating-org.narrative: The George Institute for Global Health India

recipient-country.narrative:
In South East Nigeria, we are working with the German Leprosy and TB Relief Association (DAHW) in the following projects.
1) We aim to support self-care for people in the community who are at risk of recurring leprosy ulcers, based on an ‘implementation science’ approach. We aim to Identify people at risk of ulcers from registers held in our study centres; carry out baseline assessment in ulcer prevalence and severity, and quality of life and wellbeing; build on our internationally agreed principles to design local interventions in collaboration with communities, patients, clinicians and policy-makers; pilot, refine, roll out and evaluate intervention.
2) We will conduct a cohort study to better understand the needs of Buruli Ulcer patients and the barriers to meeting those needs
3) This is one of four studies on sustainability of Self-Help Groups (SHG) once funding ceases. The aim is to evaluate post-implementation of SHG projects that were implemented in SE Nigeria in order to identify barriers and facilitators to SHG implementation/effectiveness, and the feasibility of sustaining SHG in Southern Nigeria.
4) Scoping study of traditional healers in prevention and management of leprosy and buruli ulcer. This study aims to explore the literature to determine the scope of practice and involvement of traditional healers in the prevention and management of Leprosy and Buruli ulcers.
In North Central Nigeria, we are working with the Leprosy Mission Nigeria. This is one of four studies on sustainability of Self-Help Groups (SHG) once funding ceases. We will interview different groups of people who were involved or have knowledge of the community-based self-care/self-help interventions in North Central Nigeria. The interviews will aim to explore the impact of the community-based interventions on the targeted communities.
We are also undertaking a clinical trial to evaluate the use of honey in leprosy ulcer healing.

The Leprosy Mission Trust India (TLMTI) recently proposed the replicable model project (intervention) to enhance leprosy care within the existing government health system, with the goal of reducing the rate of leprosy related disability (WHO classifications Grade I and II) below 5% in newly diagnosed children and adults in Janjgir Champa, Chhattisgarh by 2024. We will also evaluate this intervention.
Sustainability of Self-Help Groups: This is one of four studies on sustainability of Self-Help Groups (SHG) once funding ceases. We aim to evaluate the sustainability of program activities of the Self-Help Community Development Project (SHCDP) and perceptions of any short-term benefits.
Review on customised protective footwear in prevention of recurrence of ulcer in insensitive feet due to leprosy This study aims to review the literature on customised footwear and answer the following question: Does footwear with customised insole reduce the recurrence of ulcer in person affected by leprosy and diabetes at risk of ulcer as compared current standard Micro-Cellular Rubber (MCR) footwear?

The SHERPA study aims to evaluate a service intervention called Integrated Mobilization of People for Active Community Transformation (IMPACT). This is a programme funded by the government of Australia to encourage self-care and self-help. We plan to evaluate the IMPACT intervention by following a cohort of 18 self-help clusters from around the time of inception to 24 months. The study is a prospective, cluster-based, non-randomised controlled study. The IMPACT intervention will be rolled-out to 36 clusters in total, of which we will study the final 18 clusters.
We are running a clinical trial titled ‘Trial of Autologous Blood products to promote ulcer Healing in LEprosy (TABLE)'. This is a randomised clinical trial (RCT) to evaluate the efficacy of Leukocyte and Platelet-Rich Fibrin (L-PRF) on healing rates for leprosy ulcers and on duration of hospital stay.
Sustainability of Self-Help Groups: This is one of four studies on sustainability of Self-Help Groups (SHG) once funding ceases. The broad aim of the Nepal study is to evaluate the sustainability of program activities of PACED (Participatory Action for Community Empowerment and Development) and CEDAR (Community Empowerment, Development, Disability & Rehabilitation), projects run by TLMN and of perceptions any short-term benefits.

The University of Birmingham manages the overall programme of work and acts as the host contracting institution.
The University of York leads health economics and the University of Warwick leads the qualitative research components across the programme.
The Leprosy Mission International and The Leprosy Mission England and Wales provides support for the research, impact and dissemination activities.
The University of Michigan provides scientific advice and guidance across the projects.
